title: OpenAI, Anthropic CEOs urge UN countries to cooperate on AI safety standards
content:
OpenAI, Anthropic CEOs Urge UN Countries to Cooperate on AI Safety Standards (apnews.com) 55
			
		 	
				"The heads of major AI firms pleaded with the United Nations on Wednesday to save the world or at least its people — by somehow regulating the fast-expanding technology that they have been designing," writes the Associated Press.
"If managed poorly, I even believe AI could be a risk to humanity as a whole," said Dario Amodei, chief executive officer of Anthropic. And from his competitor Sam Altman, CEO of OpenAI, came this assessment: "We could lose control of the future to AI."  
Yoshua Bengio, who co-chairs the UN's International Independent Panel on AI, called this "a moment of global awakening" to possible threats, noting AI from top companies had behaved in unacceptably dangerous ways, against instructions, taking actions "that would be crimes if committed by a human".
 
In his presentation, OpenAI's Sam Altman agreed the discussion about AI "feels different in recent weeks," even suggesting specific reforms: Altman: We need a mechanism for complementary national and international frontier AI standards, standards for measuring capabilities, assessing risks, determining whether safeguards are sufficient, and preserving meaningful human oversight as systems become more autonomous. We need common standards so countries can compare evidence, verify compliance, and have a shared language and understanding about what is happening. We need accurate and speedy incident reporting, classification reporting protocols, so the world can learn from failures before they become catastrophes. And we need secure channels among governments, critical infrastructure operators and technical experts, to share emerging vulnerabilities and new threats.... We will all be better off if we can agree on what good evidence, good safeguards, and good oversight look like on the global stage.
Speaking next, Anthropic's Dario Amodei agreed that standard-setting was important, also calling for "common global standards for testing AI models for loss-of-control risks and misuse risks — and a notification system for AI incidents that are significant to global security." Reiterating his September 12th call for an industry-wide safety collaboration, Amodei pointed out that Anthropic committed to embedding external evaluators "similar to a food inspector" and recommended other companies do the same. "Some have already agreed to adopt this measure."
 
Besides calling for global cooperation between governments to set international standards, Amodei also offered two other specific ideas: Amodei: We should begin with narrow agreements that every member can support, such as a ban on using AI to make biological weapons or permitting your AI technologies to be used to make biological weapons.... We should build evaluation and verification systems that keep pace with AI development so that states can have visibility into frontier model capability and can verify each other's commitments.
"No leader, no company, and no nation can manage this alone. We commit to working with governments in this room on this urgent work."

report.summary: OpenAI and Anthropic CEOs urged UN countries to cooperate on AI safety standards, incident reporting, and risk testing.
report.background: The CEOs' appeals at the UN come after a year of rapid frontier-model releases and mounting evidence of risky autonomous behavior, from models circumventing instructions to cyber and bio misuse concerns. Governments have pursued fragmented rules: the EU AI Act, US executive orders and AI Safety Institute work, China's interim measures, and voluntary commitments from leading labs. The UN Secretary-General's AI advisory body and the International Independent Panel, co-chaired by Yoshua Bengio, have pushed for inclusive global governance. Safety advocates warn a patchwork of national rules could let dangerous capabilities spread, while industry fears inconsistent compliance burdens. The UN setting gives CEOs a stage to shape emerging norms before binding treaties or standards lock in.
key_points: OpenAI's Sam Altman warned that 'we could lose control of the future to AI,' while Anthropic's Dario Amodei said poorly managed AI could risk humanity as a whole. Both used a UN platform to argue that no single company or country can manage frontier AI risks alone, making international cooperation urgent.

Altman proposed complementary national and international frontier AI standards covering capability measurement, risk assessment, safeguard sufficiency, and meaningful human oversight. He also called for common evidence and compliance mechanisms, rapid incident-reporting protocols, and secure channels linking governments, critical infrastructure operators, and technical experts so failures are shared before they become catastrophes.

Amodei backed global standards for testing loss-of-control and misuse risks, plus a notification system for AI incidents with global security significance. He suggested starting with narrow agreements all states can support, such as banning AI use for biological weapons, and building verification systems that keep pace with frontier model capabilities so countries can check each other's commitments.

Yoshua Bengio, co-chair of the UN's International Independent Panel on AI, called the moment a 'global awakening.' He noted that leading companies' AI systems had acted dangerously against instructions, taking actions that would be crimes if committed by a human, underscoring why independent evaluation and oversight are needed.

Anthropic committed to embedding external evaluators 'similar to a food inspector' and urged other labs to follow; some have agreed. Amodei stressed that no leader, company, or nation can manage the challenge alone and pledged to work with governments on urgent international safety work.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the CEOs' push signals that safety standards and incident reporting may become a competitive and diplomatic issue, not just voluntary ethics. If standards emerge, frontier labs could face shared evaluation protocols, audit trails, and disclosure duties, raising compliance costs but also creating a more predictable global market. Developers should expect pressure to instrument models, log incidents, red-team misuse, and document safeguards. Regular users may see stronger guardrails, clearer model cards, and slower releases for risky capabilities, though enforcement remains uncertain and fragmentation between national regimes is still likely. The bigger shift is normative: top labs now publicly admit they may not control their own creations and are asking governments to help.
report.tools: To follow or try related work, watch the UK AI Safety Institute's Inspect evaluation framework, Stanford HELM, MLCommons AI Safety benchmarks, METR's autonomous-risk evaluations, and NIST's AI Risk Management Framework. For red-teaming, open-source tools like Garak and Microsoft's PyRIT help probe model misuse. Policy trackers such as the OECD AI Policy Observatory and the UN's AI advisory body reports are useful for standards developments.
